excerpt: What to do when a file opens in the wrong program, how to set the default for a file type, and why a blank white icon is not a broken file.

body.text: This lesson teaches you what to do when a file opens in the wrong program, or will not open at all. You will choose the right program, set it as the default, and recognise a white blank icon for what it is. Nothing here damages the file.

Every file has a type, written after the dot in its name. Windows uses that ending to choose a program. When the choice is wrong, or no program is registered for that ending, the file looks broken while it is perfectly fine.
Before you start

items: One file that opens in a program you did not expect.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Open it with something else, once
Start with a single opening, so you do not change the whole system for one file.

items: Right-click the file.
Choose Open with, then Choose another app.
Pick the program you want from the list.
Leave the checkbox about always using this app unticked for now.
The file opens in that program, and nothing else has changed.

body.text: You will see the program open with your file inside it, and the icon in the folder may stay the same until you set a default.

body.alt: A right-click menu showing the open with option for a file.
body.caption: Open with changes one file, once. Leave the always box unticked until you are sure.

body.text: It looks like a file that will not open is corrupt. In most cases the file is intact and has no program assigned to its type.
Set the default for a type
Once you know which program you want for a type of file, set it once and every file of that type will open there.

items: Right-click a file of that type again, and choose Open with, then Choose another app.
Select the program, then tick Always use this app.
Press OK, and the icon changes to the program's icon.
Or open Settings, then Apps, then Default apps, and set it by file type.
Test with a second file of the same type.
If you chose wrongly, repeat the steps and pick a different program.

body.text: None of this moves or edits the file. The default is a preference, and it can be changed as often as you like.

body.alt: A settings screen for choosing the default application by file type.
body.caption: The default is set per file type. Change it here, and every .docx on the machine follows.

body.text: The white blank icon
A white page icon means the machine does not know which program owns that file. The file is still there, and its contents are untouched.

items: Turn on file name extensions in View, so you can see what the file really is.
A .docx needs Word or Google Docs, not a photo viewer.
A .pdf opens in a browser if no PDF reader is installed.
A .zip needs to be extracted, not opened by double-clicking a document inside it.
A file with no ending at all may have been renamed wrongly, and can be renamed back.
A file that still will not open in any program may genuinely be damaged, which is when a backup helps.

body.text: Do not worry about installing five programs to cover every type. Two or three cover almost everything in ordinary use.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a fix, and the first two solve most of them.

items: The program is not in the list: it is not installed, or it needs updating before it registers itself.
The file opens as strange characters: the program is the wrong kind for that content, not the file.
Every file of that type now opens wrongly: repeat the default steps and choose the correct program.
The icon is still white: refresh the folder with F5, or restart the machine.
Windows asks which program every time: the default was never saved. Set it with the always box ticked.
A file you were sent will not open: ask the sender to export it as a PDF, which any machine can read.

body.text: Practice
Two files, two changes, and the mystery goes.

items: Turn on file name extensions in the View menu.
Find a file whose icon means nothing to you, and read its ending.
Open it once with a different program using Open with.
Set a default for one file type you use often.
Refresh the folder and check the icons changed.

body.text: You can now open anything you are given, and explain a white icon without alarm. In the next lesson you will read file sizes so that you can plan storage and data.

excerpt: How to read KB, MB and GB, estimate what will fit on a phone or a flash drive, and know why a 16 GB drive holds 14.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to read file sizes and storage space. You will learn what KB, MB, and GB mean, how to estimate whether a file will fit, and why a flash drive sold as 16 GB holds less. It is arithmetic you can do in your head.

A kilobyte, a megabyte, and a gigabyte are steps of about a thousand. A megabyte is roughly a thousand kilobytes, and a gigabyte is roughly a thousand megabytes. Your phone storage is counted in gigabytes, and your data bundle is often counted in megabytes.
You will see the size written beside each file in the folder, with the letters after the number deciding how big it really is.
Before you start

items: A computer with File Explorer open.
About ten minutes.

body.text: The three sizes, with examples

items: A kilobyte is a short text document, or a few sentences.
A megabyte is a photograph, a song of a few minutes, or a large document with pictures.
A gigabyte is a thousand megabytes: about three hundred photographs, or a few hundred songs.
A short video can be a hundred megabytes or more, which is why video fills a phone fastest.
An app is usually fifty to two hundred megabytes, and updates arrive at that size too.

body.text: You will see the sizes in File Explorer's size column, written as KB, MB, or GB, with the abbreviation beside the number. Sorting by size puts the largest files at the top or bottom, which is how you find what is filling the disk.

body.alt: A file window with a size column showing KB and MB values.
body.caption: Read the letters after the number. KB is small, MB is medium, and GB is a thousand times bigger.

body.text: It looks like the number matters most. The letters matter more: 2 GB is a thousand times larger than 2 MB, even though the digits look close.
Read a storage bar
Open This PC and the bar under each drive shows how full it is. That bar is the clearest answer to the question will this fit.

items: Open This PC and read the free space under the main drive.
Keep at least fifteen percent of the drive free, so the machine can work.
Sort your folders by size to find the largest and decide what to move.
A phone shows the same thing in Settings, then Storage.
Video and photographs take most of the space on most devices.
Empty the Recycle Bin after you delete large files, because they still count until then.

body.text: None of this requires a calculator. A file of 300 MB needs about a third of a gigabyte, and a drive with 2 GB free will hold it six times.

body.alt: A storage bar showing used and free space on a drive.
body.caption: The bar is the honest answer. Below about fifteen percent free, a computer starts to struggle.

body.text: Why a 16 GB drive holds 14
Manufacturers count a gigabyte as a thousand million bytes, and the operating system counts it as 1,073 million. The same space is described in two ways, which is where the missing gigabytes go.

items: A drive sold as 16 GB showing 14.9 GB is normal, not faulty.
A phone sold as 64 GB usually leaves about 50 GB for your files, because the system needs room.
A memory card's speed matters as well as its size, especially for video.
Cloud storage is counted the same way, so your free fifteen gigabytes is about fourteen on screen.
Buy storage with some headroom, because phones and computers fill up faster than people expect.

body.text: Do not worry about the missing gigabytes. Every drive does it, and no amount of formatting recovers the difference.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a practical answer, and the first one is the one people ask about.

items: The drive is full and the file is small: empty the Recycle Bin, then check Downloads.
A copy fails with a message about space: read the message, which states how much is needed.
The phone says storage is full but the list looks short: check the camera roll and app caches.
A video will not record: the phone needs about twice the video size free to write it.
A flash drive is slower than expected: cheap drives slow down on large files, which is not a fault.
Two files look the same size but one is much smaller: read the units, since one is in KB and one in MB.

body.text: Practice
Five minutes with the size column, and the numbers stop being abstract.

items: Open a folder and sort by size.
Find the largest file and read its size in the right units.
Read the free space on your main drive.
Estimate how many photographs of 4 MB would fit in 1 GB.
Delete one large file you do not need, and watch the free space change.

body.text: You can now answer whether something will fit before you start copying. In the next lesson you will use the menu that holds half the answers on a computer.

excerpt: What the right button gives you, the five actions worth knowing on any file, and how the menu changes depending on what you clicked.

body.text: This lesson explains the right-click menu. You will learn what it offers on a file, a folder, the desktop, and inside a document, and the five actions that answer most everyday questions. It is the shortest route to most settings in Windows.

The right button opens a short menu of actions that apply to whatever is under the pointer. Because it changes with context, it is the fastest way to find what you can do with a thing, without hunting through menus at the top of the window.
Before you start

items: A folder with a few files in it.
About ten minutes.

body.text: What changes with what you clicked

items: Right-click a file: open, rename, copy, cut, delete, properties, and open with.
Right-click a folder: the same, plus pinning and sharing options.
Right-click an empty space in a folder: New, View, Sort by, and Paste.
Right-click the desktop: display settings, personalise, and New.
Right-click a taskbar icon: recent files and quick actions for that program.
Right-click inside a document: paste, spelling, and formatting.

body.text: You will see a menu of between eight and twenty items, some with small arrows that open a second level. On Windows 11, you may also see Show more options at the bottom, which reveals the older menu with everything in it.

body.alt: A right-click menu open on a file in a folder.
body.caption: The menu changes with what is under the pointer. That is why the same button gives different answers in different places.

body.text: It looks like a menu that appears by accident is a fault. It is the intended behaviour, and clicking an empty space closes it without doing anything.
The five actions worth knowing
Most of what people need from this menu is one of five things. Learning these five covers the common cases.

items: Rename: changes the name without opening the file.
Properties: shows the size, the type, and where the file lives.
Copy and Paste: the same as the keyboard shortcuts, in a form you can see.
Delete: moves the file to the Recycle Bin, not into nothing.
Send to: puts a copy on the desktop, on a flash drive, or into a compressed folder.

body.text: None of these actions is dangerous, and each is reversible, either with Ctrl and Z or from the Recycle Bin.

body.alt: A person using the right mouse button on a laptop.
body.caption: On a laptop, press with two fingers on the trackpad for the same menu. Many people never discover it.

body.text: If it goes wrong
These six cases cover most of what surprises people, and each has a short answer.

items: The menu will not open: the mouse or trackpad is set for left-hand use, or the button is failing. Try two fingers on the trackpad.
The menu is very long: that is normal on a machine with many programs installed. Choose Show more options if you see it.
You clicked New by accident and a folder appeared: right-click it and delete it.
You chose Rename and the icon changed: the rename is waiting for a name. Type one and press Enter.
The menu is missing an item you expect: the program that provides it is not installed.
The menu opens in the wrong place: move the pointer to where you meant and try again.

body.text: Practice
Ten right-clicks in five places, and the menu stops being a mystery.

items: Right-click a file and open Properties.
Right-click a folder and create a new folder inside it.
Right-click an empty space and change the view to Details.
Right-click the desktop and find the display settings.
Right-click inside a document and look at the paste options.

body.text: You can now find most settings without searching for them. In the next lesson you will move a file with the mouse without losing it.

excerpt: How to move a file with the mouse without copying it by accident, what happens between drives, and how to undo a drag that went to the wrong place.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to move files with the mouse without losing them. You will learn when a drag copies and when it moves, how to be sure before you let go, and how to undo a drag that landed in the wrong folder.
Dragging a file takes it from one place and puts it in another. Whether it moves or copies depends on where it came from: within one drive it moves, and between two drives it copies.
You will see the file icon follow the pointer, and the folder under it highlight when it is ready to receive.
Before you start

items: Two folders open on screen, or one folder and the desktop.
One practice file you do not mind moving.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Drag, and watch before you let go
Nothing is lost by a drag that goes wrong, so there is no reason to fear the mouse. Press Escape or Ctrl and Z, and the file is exactly where it was.
The mouse tells you what it is about to do. Look at the small symbol beside the pointer before you release the button.

items: Click the file and hold the button down.
Move the pointer over the destination folder.
Read the small label beside the pointer: Copy to, or Move to.
Release the button to complete the action.
Press Escape before you release to cancel the drag.
Hold Ctrl while dragging to force a copy, or Shift to force a move.

body.text: You will see the folder highlight as you hover over it, and the file disappear from the first window once the drop completes. If the file is still in both places, the drag copied it, which is what happens between drives.

body.alt: A file being dragged between two folder windows.
body.caption: Hold, hover, read the label, then release. Escape cancels a drag that is going wrong.

body.text: It looks like dragging is the same everywhere. Between two drives it copies, and between two folders on one drive it moves, which is why a file sometimes stays where it was.
Move or copy on purpose
When you need certainty, use the keyboard instead of relying on the default.

items: Ctrl and C, then Ctrl and V: copies and leaves the original.
Ctrl and X, then Ctrl and V: moves and removes the original.
Both methods work across any two folders and any two drives.
Use copy for anything you are unsure about, and delete the leftover later.
For a whole folder, the same shortcuts work.
Check the destination before you close the window.

body.text: None of this is slower than dragging once you know the keys, and it removes the guesswork entirely.

body.alt: A hand dragging a file icon across a screen.
body.caption: The keyboard is the reliable version: copy, click the destination, paste, and check.

body.text: If it goes wrong
A drag that goes wrong is almost always recoverable, and the first fix works in most cases.

items: You dropped it in the wrong folder: press Ctrl and Z at once.
The file disappeared: it moved rather than copied. Search for its name, or check the folder you dragged it into.
You dropped it onto a program icon and it opened a copy: close the program, and check the file is still in its folder.
The drag will not start: you clicked outside the file, or the file is open in another program.
The pointer shows a crossed circle: the destination does not accept files, such as a program menu.
You moved a folder into itself: Windows refuses this, and the folder stays where it was.

body.text: Practice
Three drags and two keyboard moves, and the difference is clear.

items: Make two folders on the desktop, and put a test file in one.
Drag the file to the other folder and watch which label appears.
Press Ctrl and drag, and see the label change to copy.
Move a file with Ctrl and X, then Ctrl and V.
Undo one move with Ctrl and Z.

body.text: You can now move files without fear of losing them, because you know how to cancel and how to undo. In the next lesson you will write a CV that fits on one page and tells the truth.

excerpt: How to write a one-page CV with no experience gap, what to include when you are starting out, and the three things that make an employer call.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to write a one-page CV that a busy employer can read in thirty seconds. You will structure it, fill it with honest evidence, and save it as a PDF that opens anywhere. You do not need experience to have a CV worth reading.
A CV is not a life story. It is an argument that you can do the job, made in one page, with evidence a reader can check. Everything that does not support that argument is in the way of it.
If you have never written one, that is normal. Most people write their first CV in an afternoon, and nobody expects it to be finished in one draft.
Before you start

items: A document program, such as Word or Google Docs.
One quiet hour, and paper to plan on.
The dates of your schooling, any training, and any work, including informal work.

body.text: The seven parts, in order
Nigerian employers expect this order, and following it means nothing gets lost.

items: Your name, in large type, then your phone number and email address on one line.
A profile of two lines saying what you do and what you are looking for.
Education, newest first, with dates and the qualification.
Experience, newest first, including informal work, family business, and volunteering.
Skills that are true and useful, such as typing speed, Excel, or spoken languages.
One or two references, with a phone number and their permission.
Nothing else. No photograph unless the employer asks, no date of birth, no marital status.

body.text: You will see the page fill faster than you expect. If it spills onto a second page, cut the oldest schooling detail rather than shrinking the font.

body.alt: A one page CV with a clear name and short sections.
body.caption: Name, profile, education, experience, skills. One page, one font, and white space between sections.

body.text: It looks like a longer CV shows more effort. A two-page CV from a beginner usually shows padding, and a reader notices the gaps rather than the effort.
Fill it when you have little experience
Most first CVs are thin on formal work. That is normal, and it does not leave the page empty.

items: Name the work you did even if it was unpaid: helping in a family shop, teaching a younger cousin, running errands for a business.
Describe what you did with a number where you can: served about thirty customers a day.
List training and certificates, including short courses and any academy sessions completed.
Name your skills honestly: typing at 35 words a minute is stronger than fast typing.
Include school leadership, a team, or a society only if it shows something the job needs.
Leave out hobbies that say nothing about work, and leave out anything you cannot discuss if asked.

body.text: None of this is invention. The same small jobs described concretely read as experience, while a list of adjectives reads as a template.

body.alt: A printed CV on a table beside a pen.
body.caption: Print one copy and read it in your hand. Typos you missed on screen appear immediately on paper.

body.text: The three things that get a call
Employers skim. Three details decide whether they read the rest.

items: A phone number that is correct and answered politely.
Evidence that matches the job advertisement, using the words it uses.
No spelling mistakes, especially in your own name and the employer's.
A tidy layout: one font, aligned dates, and consistent spacing.
A file name that says who you are: ada-okoro-cv.pdf.
Sent as a PDF, so the layout cannot move on their computer.

body.text: Do not worry about not having the perfect background. An honest, clear, one-page CV from a beginner beats a padded one from anybody, and employers in small firms read every one.
If it goes wrong
Each of these is fixable before you send, and the last one is asked about most.

items: It will not fit on one page: cut the oldest detail, reduce the margins to 2 cm, and keep the font at 11 or 12.
The layout moves on another computer: you sent a .docx instead of a PDF.
You have no references: ask a teacher, a pastor, or a former customer, and ask their permission first.
You cannot remember exact dates: use the month and the year, which is accurate enough.
The file is too large to email: it probably contains photographs. Remove them, or export again.
You have a gap in your dates: state it honestly, such as caring for a family member, rather than filling it with a false entry.

body.text: Practice
Write it in one sitting, then leave it a day before you send it.

items: Write the seven sections on paper first, with dates.
Type it in Word with one font at 11 or 12 point.
Cut it to one page, and check the margins.
Save it as a PDF named with your own name.
Print one copy, read it aloud, and ask somebody else to read it too.

body.text: You can now hand an employer a page that respects their time and gives them a reason to call. In the next chapter the series moves to the shop counter, where a spreadsheet earns its keep.
